chapters.title: Chapter 4: Trading Forex Legally in India

lessons.title: What Is Legal and What Is Not: FEMA, LRS and the RBI Alert List

children.text: OctaFX looked like a real broker. It had a slick app, round-the-clock chat support and paid promotions by well-known TV actors. Thousands of Indians deposited money through UPI and traded currencies and gold with high leverage. Then came a Pune Police FIR, Enforcement Directorate raids and, eventually, attachment of assets worth about ₹2,681 crore, including cryptocurrency, properties and a yacht. Many users could not get their money back, and they had no regulator to complain to. This lesson draws the legal line clearly: which currency transactions an Indian resident can make, through whom, for what purpose, and how to spot a platform that will put both your money and your legal standing at risk.

body.text: A forex transaction is legal for an Indian resident only when three things line up: the right counterparty (an RBI-authorised person or a recognised Indian exchange), the right channel, and a permitted purpose. Miss any one of the three and the deal is outside the law, no matter how professional the app looks.

markDefs.definition: A bank, money changer or other entity authorised by RBI under FEMA to deal in foreign exchange. Most commercial banks are Authorised Dealers.
An electronic platform for trading foreign exchange or rupee derivatives. Offering one to Indian residents requires RBI authorisation.

children.text: The Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, or FEMA, is the law that governs every rupee that crosses India's border. Its core rule is simple: a resident can deal in foreign exchange only with an
, and only for purposes the law permits. RBI writes the detailed rules. It also authorises the

that may offer forex products to Indian residents. SEBI regulates the stock exchanges where currency derivatives are listed. An offshore app is neither an authorised person nor an authorised platform for Indian residents.

body.caption: Who does what in India's forex rulebook

cells: Parliament, through FEMA 1999
Sets the law on foreign exchange
Unauthorised forex dealing can attract penalties
RBI
Writes the rules, authorises dealers and platforms, publishes the Alert List
Only RBI-authorised entities can deal forex with you
SEBI
Regulates NSE, BSE and brokers that offer currency derivatives
Exchange-traded contracts come with investor protection and grievance routes
Enforcement Directorate
Investigates FEMA and money laundering violations
Illegal platforms and their promoters can face raids and asset attachment

body.label: Penalty for contravening FEMA
body.value: Up to three times the amount involved
body.context: Where the amount can be quantified. Otherwise up to ₹2 lakh, plus up to ₹5,000 for every day a contravention continues. FEMA is a civil law, but related money laundering cases can bring far more serious consequences.

children.text: LRS: Your Legal Window to Send Money Abroad

markDefs.definition: The Liberalised Remittance Scheme. It lets resident individuals send up to $250,000 abroad each financial year for permitted current and capital account purposes.

children.text: is how most Indians legally move money abroad, whether for a child's tuition in Canada, a Europe holiday or buying Apple shares through an overseas investing app. But LRS is a list of permitted purposes, not a blank cheque. Using it to fund leveraged currency trading abroad is specifically not allowed.

body.label: LRS limit per resident individual
body.context: Covers all permitted purposes combined, remitted through an Authorised Dealer bank. Tax collected at source (TCS) may apply above a threshold, depending on the purpose.

body.title: What LRS allows vs what it does not

columns.label: Permitted under LRS
points: Education, travel and medical expenses abroad
Gifts and maintenance of close relatives abroad
Buying foreign shares, ETFs and mutual funds outright
Opening a foreign currency account abroad for permitted transactions

columns.label: Not permitted under LRS
points: Margin trading or paying margin calls to overseas exchanges or brokers
Buying FCCBs issued abroad by Indian companies
Remittances to countries RBI or FATF identify as non-cooperative

body.title: The LRS limit in rupees
body.prompt: At USD/INR 95.50, what is the full $250,000 LRS limit worth in rupees? Give the answer in lakh rupees, rounded to two decimals.
body.explanation: $250,000 × 95.50 = ₹2,38,75,000, or ₹238.75 lakh (₹2.39 crore). Because the limit is fixed in dollars, a weaker rupee raises the rupee value of what you can remit, though the dollar limit itself does not change.

body.title: A note on TCS for LRS remittances

children.text: Banks collect tax at source, or TCS, on LRS remittances above an annual threshold, which has been ₹10 lakh for most purposes. The rate depends on the purpose: investments and general remittances above the threshold have attracted 20%, while education and medical remittances have lower rates. TCS is not an extra tax. It is an advance that you can claim as a credit against your income tax or get refunded when you file your return. Rates have changed in recent Union Budgets, so confirm the current rate with your bank before remitting.
The Exchange Route: Legal, With Conditions

markDefs.definition: An actual or anticipated foreign currency risk that a hedge protects against, such as dollar export receivables, import payments or a foreign currency loan.

children.text: Currency futures and options are listed on NSE and BSE and traded through SEBI-registered brokers. This is the regulated, exchange-traded route. But there is a condition most beginners miss. Since RBI's directions took effect on 3 May 2024, contracts involving the rupee, such as USD/INR, EUR/INR, GBP/INR and JPY/INR, may be used only by participants with a genuine
to the currency. RBI has not changed this position since.

body.caption: Legal routes for currency transactions in India and their conditions

cells: Rupee-pair derivatives on NSE and BSE
USD/INR, EUR/INR, GBP/INR, JPY/INR futures and options
Must have a genuine currency exposure being hedged. No documents needed up to $100 million across exchanges, but the exposure must exist.
Cross-currency derivatives on NSE and BSE
EUR/USD, GBP/USD, USD/JPY futures and options
Positions allowed without establishing an underlying exposure, within exchange position limits
Forwards and options with an Authorised Dealer bank
Exporter booking a 3-month forward
Genuine exposure, documented as the bank requires
CCIL FX-Retail platform, through your bank
Buying dollars for tuition
Genuine forex requirement
LRS remittance through an Authorised Dealer bank
Buying US shares outright, paying overseas fees

body.text: The $100 million "no documentation" limit is widely misread. It means you do not have to show paperwork for positions up to that size. It does not mean you can trade rupee pairs without any exposure. RBI said explicitly in 2024 that treating the relaxation as permission to trade without an exposure is a violation. A salaried professional with no foreign currency receivables, payments or loans cannot legally speculate in USD/INR futures just because no broker asks for proof.

body.title: Who can trade USD/INR futures?
body.question: Under RBI's rules for exchange-traded currency derivatives involving the rupee, which of these participants can legally sell USD/INR futures on NSE?
options: Aditya, a salaried analyst in Pune with no foreign currency income or payments, who thinks the rupee will strengthen
A Surat diamond exporter expecting $80,000 from a Belgian buyer in two months, hedging against a stronger rupee
Anyone, as long as the position is below $100 million
A college student using a demo strategy from a Telegram group
body.explanation: The exporter has a genuine dollar receivable and is hedging it, which is exactly what the rules allow. Aditya and the student have no underlying exposure. The $100 million limit only waives documentation. It does not remove the need for a real exposure.

children.text: What Is Clearly Illegal: Offshore Forex Apps

Offshore platforms offering leveraged trading in currency pairs, gold, indices or "CFDs" to Indian residents are not authorised by RBI. Because LRS does not permit margin trading or trading forex abroad, residents also have no legal way to fund such accounts. Many of these platforms collect deposits through UPI or local bank accounts that belong to individuals or shell entities, precisely to avoid the banking system's checks. RBI has said that residents dealing with unauthorised entities make themselves liable to penal action under FEMA.

body.label: RBI Alert List of unauthorised forex platforms
body.context: As of the November 2025 update, which added seven platforms including Starnet FX, CapPlace, Mirrox, Fusion Markets, Trive, NXG Markets and Nord FX. RBI says the list is not exhaustive.

body.title: The Crackdown on Illegal Forex Platforms

events.title: Alert List launched
events.description: RBI publishes its first Alert List of entities that are neither authorised to deal in forex nor to operate forex trading platforms, and warns residents against using them.

events.title: Regular expansion
events.description: RBI adds names in batches, including websites and social media accounts that promote unauthorised platforms or sell forex "training" and signals.

events.title: ED investigates OctaFX
events.description: Following a Pune Police FIR, the Enforcement Directorate searches premises in several cities and questions celebrities who promoted the app.

events.title: Large asset attachment
events.description: ED attaches cryptocurrency and other assets, taking the total attached in the case to about ₹2,681 crore, including 19 properties and a yacht.

body.caption: Red flags of an illegal forex platform

cells: Deposits by UPI to an individual's name or a random company
Legitimate brokers collect money into designated client accounts, not personal accounts
Leverage of 1:100, 1:500 or higher on EUR/USD, gold or indices
Indian exchanges set far lower leverage through margins; extreme leverage is a hallmark of offshore CFD platforms
Regulated "abroad" but no RBI authorisation or SEBI registration
A licence in another country does not permit dealing with Indian residents
Celebrity or influencer promotions, referral bonuses and "signal" groups
Promoters of unauthorised platforms also appear on the Alert List and have been questioned by ED
Withdrawals delayed, capped or conditional on further deposits
Classic sign that customer money is not safe or not there

body.title: Before you deal with any forex platform
steps: Search the platform, its app name and its promoters on RBI's Alert List.
Check RBI's list of authorised electronic trading platforms and authorised persons.
If it offers exchange-traded contracts, confirm the broker is SEBI-registered and the contracts trade on NSE or BSE.
For rupee pairs, confirm you have a genuine currency exposure to hedge.
Refuse any request to deposit money by UPI to an individual or unrelated company.
Remember the Alert List is not exhaustive: a missing name does not mean a platform is legal.

body.title: Legal or not?
body.scenario: Six people describe what they are doing. (a) Neha in Bengaluru remits $20,000 under LRS through her bank to buy a US index ETF outright. (b) Rakesh in Indore deposits ₹50,000 by UPI into an offshore app to trade gold and EUR/USD with 1:500 leverage. (c) A Coimbatore textile exporter with $150,000 of receivables due in three months sells USD/INR futures on NSE. (d) Sameer, a salaried engineer with no foreign currency income or payments, buys USD/INR futures, saying "no documents are needed under $100 million." (e) Tanya trades EUR/USD cross-currency futures on NSE through her SEBI-registered broker, within exchange limits. (f) Kunal remits money under LRS to an overseas broker to meet margin calls on a leveraged forex account.
body.prompt: Classify each as legal or not legal under the rules in this lesson, and give the reason in one line.
body.modelAnswer:
(a) Legal. Buying foreign ETFs outright is a permitted LRS purpose, within the $250,000 limit, subject to TCS rules.
(b) Not legal. The app is not RBI-authorised, and residents cannot fund leveraged offshore forex or CFD trading. UPI deposits to such platforms are a classic red flag.
(c) Legal. The exporter has a genuine dollar exposure and is hedging it with a rupee-pair contract on a recognised exchange.
(d) Not legal. The $100 million limit only waives documentation. Trading rupee pairs without an underlying exposure is a violation that RBI has specifically called out.
(e) Legal. Residents may take positions in cross-currency contracts on Indian exchanges without establishing an underlying exposure, within exchange position limits.
(f) Not legal. LRS does not permit remittances for margin trading or margin calls abroad, or for trading in foreign exchange abroad.

body.title: The LRS limit
body.textWithBlank: Under LRS, a resident individual can remit up to $___ per financial year for permitted purposes.
body.explanation: The LRS limit is $250,000 per financial year per resident individual, covering all permitted purposes combined.

cards.definition: The Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999. Residents may deal in forex only with authorised persons and for permitted purposes.
An entity, such as an Authorised Dealer bank, permitted by RBI to deal in foreign exchange.
Liberalised Remittance Scheme. Up to $250,000 a year abroad for permitted purposes. Margin trading and forex trading abroad are not permitted.
A genuine currency risk being hedged. Required to use rupee-pair derivatives on NSE and BSE since 3 May 2024.
Positions in rupee-pair derivatives up to this size need no documents, but a real exposure must still exist.
RBI's non-exhaustive list of unauthorised forex platforms and promoters. 95 names as of November 2025.

points: Under FEMA, residents can deal in forex only with RBI-authorised persons, through permitted channels, for permitted purposes.
Contravening FEMA can attract penalties of up to three times the amount involved.
LRS allows up to $250,000 a year for purposes like education, travel and buying foreign shares outright, but not margin trading or forex trading abroad.
Rupee-pair derivatives on NSE and BSE are legal only for participants with a genuine currency exposure. The $100 million limit waives documents, not the exposure.
Cross-currency contracts like EUR/USD on Indian exchanges can be traded by residents without an underlying exposure, within exchange limits.
Offshore leveraged forex and CFD apps are not a legal route for residents. RBI's Alert List had 95 names by November 2025 and is not exhaustive.
Check the Alert List, RBI's authorised lists and SEBI registration before dealing with any platform.

body.text: This lesson is for general education only and is not legal, tax or investment advice. Rules under FEMA, LRS, RBI's derivatives directions and tax laws change from time to time. Check the latest RBI directions, SEBI circulars and Income Tax provisions, and consult a qualified professional before acting. Details of enforcement cases are based on public reports and allegations under investigation.
